title: What is a SOC?
summary: The function, the structure and the daily reality of a security operations centre.

sections.p: A Security Operations Centre is the function responsible for detecting, investigating and responding to security events across an organisation. It is a capability rather than a room: people, process and tooling combined so that suspicious activity is noticed, understood and acted on continuously.

Monitoring telemetry from endpoints, servers, network devices, identity platforms and cloud services. Triaging detections into real, benign or needs-more-work. Investigating the real ones. Containing what is confirmed. Feeding everything learned back into detection content.

Almost all work arrives as a queue of detections raised by correlation rules, EDR behavioural analytics, mail security, DLP and user reports. A mature SOC also generates work proactively through threat hunting, where the analyst starts from a hypothesis rather than an alert.

Coverage is usually 24/7 through follow-the-sun or rotating shifts. Handover between shifts is a formal process: open cases, active escalations, pending actions and anything a colleague must chase. Handover failures are one of the most common causes of long detection-to-action gaps.

Short time to triage, short time to contain, a false positive rate low enough that analysts have attention left for real work, detection coverage measured against a framework, and every escalation with a named owner. Volume of alerts closed is not a quality measure.

A SOC is not a wall that stops attacks. It is the function that finds what got past the walls, reduces the damage, and makes the walls better next time. Measuring a SOC by whether incidents happen is measuring the wrong thing; measure it by how quickly they are found and how far they get.

title: SOC Analyst Roles
summary: Who does what in a SOC, and how the roles interact during an incident.

sections.p: Tier 1 triages the queue and performs initial investigation. Tier 2 investigates escalations in depth and drives containment. Tier 3 handles the hardest cases, threat hunting and forensics. Alongside them sit detection engineers who build and tune rules, threat intelligence analysts who track actors, and incident managers who coordinate response and communication.

Owns the incident rather than the analysis: sequencing, stakeholder communication, legal and regulatory engagement, and the decision to invoke crisis process. During a major incident the analyst supplies facts and recommendations; the incident manager decides and records.

Infrastructure and platform teams execute most containment actions (firewall changes, account disabling, host isolation). Identity teams own credential resets. Legal and privacy own breach notification. The SOC rarely has unilateral authority over production, which is why precise, well-evidenced recommendations matter more than access.

Threat intelligence should change decisions. If an actor profile says exfiltration precedes extortion within 72 hours, that changes the urgency of containment. Intelligence that only decorates a report is wasted effort.

Most analysts enter at Tier 1 and move toward one of three directions: deeper investigation and forensics, detection engineering, or incident management. All three benefit from the same foundation - the ability to read raw telemetry and reason from evidence.

title: Tier 1 / Tier 2 / Tier 3
summary: What each tier is accountable for, and how to escalate well.

sections.p: Work the queue in risk order, determine true or false positive with evidence, contain obvious cases within delegated authority, escalate anything touching critical assets or exceeding delegated scope, and document everything so the next person can continue without asking.

Deep investigation across multiple data sources, scoping (how many hosts, how many identities), attribution support, containment planning, and the technical narrative that goes into the incident report.

Forensics, malware analysis, threat hunting, complex correlation, and the detection content that comes out of an incident. Tier 3 also validates whether detections actually fire, usually through purple team exercises.

State what you observed, what you concluded, what evidence supports it, what you have already done, and what you need. An escalation that says 'this looks bad, please look' transfers work without transferring understanding.

Any confirmed activity on a Tier-0 asset, any evidence of domain-level credential compromise, any confirmed data movement, any impact-stage activity such as shadow copy deletion or backup tampering. These do not wait for the end of your analysis.
Escalating everything, or escalating nothing. Both are failures of judgement. The measure is whether a Tier-2 analyst receiving your escalation would agree it needed them.

title: Alert Triage
summary: The decision layer between detection and investigation.

sections.p: Is the observed behaviour real? Is it authorised? Does it need escalation? Every triage decision is an answer to those three, supported by a named artefact.

Rank by risk, not by arrival order or by the severity label the tool printed. Risk combines the severity of the behaviour with the criticality of the asset and the identity involved. A MEDIUM detection on a domain controller outranks a HIGH on a lab VM.
A false positive closure must name the evidence: a change ticket, a deployment job, a signed binary from an expected path, a documented business process. 'Looked fine' is not a closure.
Byte-identical command lines across many hosts within minutes, a signed management agent as the parent process, and no outbound network activity almost always mean software deployment, not intrusion.

Unsigned binaries in user-writable paths, execution chains that begin with a user document or shortcut, authentication from infrastructure with no business relationship, and behaviour that continues after the initial event.
Record the alert ID, the verdict, the evidence, the action taken and any tuning request. The tuning request is what stops the same alert consuming the next shift too.
Triaging alerts individually when they are one campaign. Before closing, check whether the same source, account or host appears elsewhere in the queue.

title: Log Analysis
summary: Reading raw telemetry without a dashboard in front of you.

sections.p: Dashboards normalise and therefore lose detail. Field names differ between vendors; the underlying event does not. An analyst who can read raw Windows events, syslog, firewall logs and flow records can work anywhere.
When, where, who, what and from where. Timestamp, host, account, action, source address. If a log line does not answer those, find the source that does.
Suspicion requires a norm. Before calling something anomalous, know what the account, host or service does on an ordinary day - working hours, source addresses, typical volume.
Normalise everything to UTC and state the timezone in every finding. Mixed timezones produce sequences that look causal but are not, and that error survives into reports.
Counts are evidence. Twelve failed logons is a finding; 'several failures' is an impression. Count precisely and state the window the count covers.
Reading only the alerting event. The events immediately before and after it usually carry the actual story - especially anything that happens after a successful authentication.

title: SIEM
summary: Correlation, search and the analyst workflow inside a SIEM.

sections.p: Collects logs from many sources, normalises them into common fields, retains them for search, and runs correlation rules that raise detections when patterns match.

Scope a time window. Filter to relevant sources. Pivot on an entity - an IP, user, host or hash. Aggregate to find outliers. Correlate across sources to build the sequence. Repeat with each new entity discovered.

Pivoting is the skill that separates search from investigation. One confirmed indicator searched across every index produces more than ten alert reviews, because each hit generates the next search term.

Counts by source, distinct destinations per account, events per minute. Outliers surface through aggregation far faster than through reading. 'Distinct hosts authenticated to per account per hour' catches lateral movement that no single event reveals.

Rules join events across sources - for example, a failed logon burst followed by a success from the same address, followed by process creation on the target. Poorly written joins produce spurious matches, so always verify the underlying events.
Record every query with its time window. A count without a window cannot be reproduced, and an unreproducible number does not belong in a report.

title: EDR
summary: Endpoint detection and response as an investigation tool.

sections.p: Process creation with full command lines and parent relationships, file writes, registry modifications, module loads, network connections and in many products memory events - all linked into a process tree.
The tree is the investigation. Work outward from the alerting process: what started it, what it started, what it wrote, what it contacted. Most endpoint cases resolve entirely within the tree.

Unsigned binaries, execution from user-writable paths, impossible parent-child relationships, system binary names running from the wrong directory, and processes making outbound connections to raw IP addresses.

Network isolation (the host stays up for investigation but cannot reach anything except the console), process termination, file quarantine, and blocking by hash or path across the estate. Isolation preserves evidence; shutdown destroys memory.

Coverage is rarely complete - Linux, network appliances, OT and unmanaged devices are often blind spots. An intrusion that begins where EDR is not installed will be invisible until it reaches a covered host.
Trusting the product's verdict instead of reading the tree. EDR severity is an input to your judgement, not a replacement for it.

title: Network Monitoring
summary: Reading behaviour from traffic when you cannot read content.

sections.p: Flow records (NetFlow, IPFIX), firewall session logs, proxy logs, DNS resolver logs, TLS metadata and Zeek-style connection summaries. Full packet capture exists in some environments but is rarely available retrospectively.

Encryption hides payload but not behaviour. How often, how long, how much, in which direction, and to where - these five properties identify beaconing, exfiltration, scanning and tunnelling without decrypting anything.

Regular intervals with small, symmetric payloads. Jitter is added deliberately to defeat visual inspection, so average the intervals rather than eyeballing them. A ten-minute cadence that matches a scheduled task on the host is conclusive.
Far more out than in suggests exfiltration; far more in than out suggests tool download. Neither is conclusive alone - backup replication and software updates produce both patterns legitimately.

Certificate details (self-signed, CN=localhost, recently issued), SNI, and client fingerprints such as JA3 identify tooling even when the content is opaque. A fingerprint shared across unrelated destinations often reveals the same operator.
A compromised host with no internet route is still being controlled. Look for internal pivots: SMB named pipes, internal HTTP proxies, or a relay host that has both internal reach and egress.

title: Windows Security
summary: The event IDs and artefacts that matter most on Windows.

sections.p: 4624 successful logon, 4625 failed logon, 4634 logoff, 4648 logon with explicit credentials, 4672 special privileges assigned, 4740 account lockout. Logon types: 2 interactive, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service, 10 RemoteInteractive (RDP).

On 4625, 0xC000006A means the account exists but the password was wrong (password guessing) and 0xC0000064 means the account does not exist (username enumeration). 0xC000015B means the logon type was not granted - usually a segmentation or policy control working as intended.
4688 process creation with parent and command line; 4104 PowerShell script block logging, which records code after de-obfuscation and is the single most valuable execution artefact on Windows.

4720 account created, 4722 enabled, 4724 password reset, 4726 deleted, 4728 added to a global group, 4732 added to a local group, 4738 account changed. The Subject field is who did it; the Target field is to whom.
7045 service installed, 5140 and 5145 network share access. A 7045 with an unsigned binary outside System32 and Program Files is one of the highest-fidelity indicators available.
1102 records that the security log was cleared. An absence of records is itself evidence, and volume shadow copies frequently preserve what was cleared.

title: Linux Security
summary: Authentication, execution and persistence evidence on Linux systems.

sections.p: /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure for SSH and sudo, the systemd journal for service events, auditd where deployed, shell history files, cron tables, systemd units and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

'Failed password for invalid user X' means the account does not exist - enumeration. 'Failed password for root' means it does. 'Accepted password' on a host that should be key-only is itself a finding. Sequential source ports across attempts indicate an automated tool.
sudo entries record TTY, working directory, target user and the exact COMMAND. Reading sudo history after a suspicious login is usually the fastest route to understanding what the intruder did.

cron and systemd timers, systemd unit files, rc scripts, shell profiles, SUID binaries, and additional entries in authorized_keys. A new key with an innocuous comment is a common and easily missed backdoor.

'history -c' clears the in-memory buffer but does not remove what has already been written to the history file, and it does not touch auth.log or the journal. Hidden files in /tmp and /dev/shm are a standard habit worth checking explicitly.

Linux telemetry is frequently weaker than Windows in enterprise estates. Where auditd or EDR coverage is partial, assume investigation will depend on text logs and filesystem timestamps, and raise the gap as a finding.
